deck.headline: Bank of England cuts UK bank capital requirements and warns AI borrowing links risks together
deck.sub: Tier 1 needs fall by about 0.5 points of risk-weighted assets; hyperscaler bonds pass $305bn this year
deck.summary: The Bank of England finished its capital review: major UK banks' Tier 1 requirements fall by about half a percentage point of risk-weighted assets, with an overall benchmark near 13%. It also warned that AI borrowing, including over $305 billion of hyperscaler bonds this year, ties risks together, and that AI agents raise cyber risk.
deck.whyItMatters: UK lenders get room to lend or return capital, but supervisors want to see where AI-linked exposures sit and how fast banks can recover from cyber incidents; expect questions on both in 2027 reviews.
deck.checked: Checked on the Bank of England's November 2026 Financial Stability Report page (opened)
deck.storyline: Storyline: bank capital and risk controls · day 3
deck.detailHtml:
The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee published its November Financial Stability Report on 26 Nov and closed its review of bank capital. The PRA will consult on lower minimum requirements for domestic lending, which together with earlier changes cut Tier 1 capital requirements for major UK banks by about 50 basis points of risk-weighted assets in normal times, with further relief in stress scenarios. System-wide requirements will sit at the FPC's updated benchmark of around 13%, and the neutral countercyclical buffer stays at 2%. The FPC says going much further 'would risk financial instability'.

The same report warns that AI-related financing now spans equities, public bonds, private credit and 'circular' vendor-financing deals: hyperscaler bond issuance is set to exceed $305bn in 2026, about 8% of global investment-grade issuance. It says frontier AI agents and open-weight models make cyber and operational risk a more prominent threat, and asks firms to speed up quantum-safe cryptography.

Twice a year the Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee sets out the risks to the UK financial system. This report did two things at once. It finished a review the government wanted, aimed at freeing banks to lend more: minimum requirements tied to domestic lending will fall, so the biggest UK banks need roughly half a percentage point less Tier 1 capital against their risk-weighted assets, and the committee's overall benchmark settles at about 13%. It also drew a line: cutting much further would weaken banks' ability to absorb shocks.

The risk section is where AI comes in. Borrowing to build data centres is growing fast and spreading across bonds, private credit and complex vendor-financing loops, which makes it harder to see who ultimately holds the risk. The committee also says more capable AI agents and open-weight models raise the bar for cyber defence, and that the shift to quantum-resistant cryptography should start now.

deck.headline: SAP confirms hackers got into its GitHub development systems; signing keys replaced
deck.summary: SAP confirmed a cyber incident after reports that attackers stole staff GitHub tokens and could copy and change its source code. SAP restricted GitHub, paused automated builds and replaced its software-signing keys. It has not said whether any shipped code was altered, which matters to the many banks running SAP.
deck.whyItMatters: SAP runs core ledgers, payroll and treasury at most large banks. Ask SAP whether any patches or packages were signed with the old keys, and check that your update channels pin the new ones.
deck.checked: Checked on The Record, SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer (opened); Der Spiegel report is paywalled
deck.storyline: Storyline: attacks through software and vendors · day 13
deck.detailHtml: SAP confirmed on Friday that it is investigating a cyber incident after Der Spiegel reported that attackers obtained employees' authentication tokens for SAP's development environment on GitHub, which let them copy and modify source code. According to The Record, SAP has restricted GitHub access, halted automated development processes and replaced the digital keys it uses to prove its software is genuine. Handelsblatt says the response is code-named 'Project Granite'. SAP says it moved immediately to protect customers; it has not said whether any shipped code was altered.

deck.headline: Hackers breached the US Air Force cloud that runs air-defence and munitions systems
deck.summary: Reuters reports hackers breached Cloud One, the US Air Force's shared cloud built on Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Google, through an unknown software flaw. It hosts air-defence radar and munitions-tracking systems. It is the fourth reported US federal breach in about two weeks, after FinCEN, the FBI and the CIA. No attribution yet.
deck.whyItMatters: No attribution yet, but a run of federal breaches through shared platforms is exactly the concentration risk the Bank of England flagged the same week; expect new CISA directives.
deck.checked: Checked on BleepingComputer, Decrypt and SiliconANGLE (opened), all citing Reuters
deck.storyline: Storyline: hacks on US government systems · day 4
deck.detailHtml: Attackers got into Cloud One, the US Air Force's shared cloud platform, by exploiting an unidentified software vulnerability, Reuters reports. The breach was found within the past month during an upgrade and disrupted application migrations and software updates. Cloud One, launched in 2017, pools Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Google clouds; per Decrypt it hosts the Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control (air-defence radar feeds across North America) and a system that tracks munitions at more than 200 bases. The Air Force declined to comment. It is the fourth reported US federal breach in about two weeks, after FinCEN, the FBI's NCIC database and a CIA open-source intelligence system.

deck.headline: Pablo Hernández de Cos, head of the BIS, will run the ECB from February
deck.summary: Euro zone governments picked Pablo Hernández de Cos, head of the BIS and former Bank of Spain governor, to replace Christine Lagarde at the ECB. Reuters says he takes over on 7 February and chairs his first rate meeting on 18 March. Markets expect continuity and a firm hand on bank rules.
deck.whyItMatters: A Basel veteran at the ECB means continuity on rates and a supervisor who knows the bank-capital rules by heart; markets read him as willing to backstop sovereign debt, which matters with France's rating outlook now negative.
deck.storyline: Storyline: who runs the central banks · day 2
deck.detailHtml: Euro zone countries have chosen Pablo Hernández de Cos, 55, the BIS general manager and former governor of the Bank of Spain, to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president. The race ended on 26 Nov when Dutch rival Klaas Knot congratulated him. Reuters, cited by FintechNews, says Lagarde steps down early on 7 Feb 2027 and de Cos chairs his first rate meeting on 18 March; the deal also fills two Executive Board seats for Germany and France. He ran Spain's central bank through the Covid shock and the 2022-23 rate rises and chaired the Basel Committee.

deck.headline: OpenAI countersues Apple, accusing it of stealing device secrets and pressuring suppliers
deck.summary: OpenAI countersued Apple in California, saying Apple stole its device secrets by rehiring an employee who had seen its hardware roadmap, and pressured suppliers that work with both companies. It answers Apple's July lawsuit over designers who joined OpenAI. Apple had said it found no OpenAI files.
deck.whyItMatters: The fight is now about access to the Asian supply chain for AI devices, not just hiring; component makers serving both firms may face discovery and pressure to pick sides.
deck.storyline: Storyline: OpenAI and Apple's legal fight · day 2
deck.detailHtml: OpenAI filed counterclaims against Apple in California federal court, the FT and Reuters report. It says Apple gained confidential information by rehiring an employee who had spent six months at OpenAI with access to a new device and its hardware roadmap, and that Apple is 'coercing and threatening' suppliers that also work with OpenAI. OpenAI says its devices threaten to 'outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf'. The filing answers Apple's July suit against OpenAI, io Products and two former Apple designers. Apple said in October its investigation had found no OpenAI files.

deck.headline: US disables a ship running its Iran blockade; drones kill two Italians in Kuwait
deck.summary: US Central Command said its aircraft disabled the Pacific Archer as it tried to leave Iran through the US blockade. Iran vowed to keep the Strait of Hormuz shut. Drones that Italy and Kuwait say were Iranian killed two Italian technicians at a Kuwaiti base; Iran denies it.
deck.whyItMatters: Hormuz stays effectively closed going into Sunday's OPEC+ meeting, keeping oil near $90 and feeding the energy-driven inflation the Bank of England and Fed are worried about.
deck.storyline: Storyline: the Iran war and the economy · day 11
deck.detailHtml: US aircraft struck the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman after it sailed from Bandar Abbas, disabling its propulsion without hurting the crew, US Central Command said; it was trying to run the naval blockade of Iranian ports the US reimposed in July. An adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader said Tehran would keep the Strait of Hormuz shut and break the embargo. Separately, Iranian-made drones hit Kuwaiti military installations on Thursday, killing two Italian technicians from Rheinmetall, Italy and Kuwait said; Iran's foreign minister denied involvement. Iran has stepped up attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain this week.

deck.headline: RBI eases daily cash-reserve rule as liquidity turns tight, and sets money-mule account holds
deck.summary: India's central bank cut the daily cash-reserve minimum back to 90% from 99% from 1 December, as banking liquidity slipped into a deficit of about Rs 47,600 crore. It also gave banks a standard way to freeze suspected money-mule accounts from July 2027, and let white-label ATM firms buy cash from any bank.
deck.whyItMatters: The CRR change frees short-term funding for treasuries into year-end; the mule-account SOP gives fraud teams legal cover to freeze first, but they must build the release process with law enforcement.
deck.storyline: Storyline: how India's RBI supervises banks · day 8
deck.detailHtml: The RBI reversed its October tightening: from 1 Dec banks need to hold only 90% of required cash reserves on any day, not 99%, with the overall CRR unchanged at 3%. Mint says system liquidity has swung from a surplus of about Rs 11 trillion in mid-September to a deficit of Rs 47,641 crore on 26 Nov, as forex intervention and government cash balances drained funds. The same day the RBI issued final directions giving banks a standard procedure to put temporary debit holds on accounts suspected of money-mule activity, coordinated with police, effective 1 July 2027 (earlier if a bank chooses). It also let white-label ATM operators buy cash from any bank, or directly from RBI issue offices, and merged 17 ATM and PoS cash-withdrawal circulars.

deck.headline: Unpatched Cacti flaw with public exploit lets anyone run commands on monitoring servers
deck.summary: A researcher published a working exploit for an unpatched flaw in Cacti, a widely used network-monitoring tool, that runs commands on the server without logging in. Cacti often stores credentials for routers and firewalls. There is no patch yet, so cutting off access to Cacti's web interface is the stopgap.
deck.whyItMatters: Take Cacti web interfaces off any network an attacker could reach today and rotate the stored SNMP credentials; with public code, scanning will start within days.
deck.storyline: Storyline: critical patches to apply now · day 4
deck.detailHtml: A researcher disclosed an unpatched flaw in Cacti, the open-source tool many IT teams use to graph servers, routers and firewalls, and published a working exploit: from an unauthenticated web session to command execution in four requests, BleepingComputer reports. Because Cacti often stores the SNMP credentials it uses to poll network gear, a compromised server can open the way to the rest of the network. No fix has been released.

deck.headline: Black Friday card skimmer hid in WebRTC on Samsonite, Revolve and three other stores
deck.summary: Researchers at InfoHawk found a card skimmer on the Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve, FWRD and Lascana online stores before Black Friday. It hid in WebRTC, the video-call channel many security tools ignore, and sent a test card to a third party. Revolve says it fixed its sites on 25 November; victim numbers are unknown.
deck.whyItMatters: Issuers should watch for card-not-present fraud on cards used at these merchants this month; merchants should add WebRTC to their content-security policies.
deck.detailHtml: Security firm InfoHawk found a card-skimming script on the online stores of Lascana, Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve and FWRD in the week before Black Friday. The script used WebRTC, the browser technology behind video calls, both to load itself and to send card details out, because many security tools do not watch that channel. InfoHawk saw its test card sent to a third party on Lascana. Revolve says it fixed the issue on its mobile and tablet sites the day it was told (25 Nov). How many shoppers were hit is unknown.
deck.sourcesHtml: OFFICIALInfoHawk: card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sitesOTHERHacker News discussion (404 points)

deck.headline: Russia's Sber releases GigaChat 4, a 708B open model with a million-token context
deck.summary: Sber's GigaChat team released GigaChat 4 under the MIT licence: a 708-billion-parameter model that uses 41 billion per token, reads up to a million tokens and switches between quick and reasoning modes. Its own tests score 80.9 on SWE-bench Verified. Weights, base model and training checkpoints are all public.
deck.whyItMatters: A bank-built model at the open frontier, with checkpoints researchers can study; Western banks will not deploy a Russian model, but it shows how far in-house bank AI can go.
deck.storyline: Storyline: how good open models get · day 28
deck.detailHtml: The GigaChat team at Russia's largest bank, Sber, has published GigaChat 4 on Hugging Face under the MIT licence: 708B parameters, 41B active per token, mixing linear attention (Gated DeltaNet) with DeepSeek-style sparse attention for a 1M-token context, and offering instant and reasoning modes in one model. Its own evaluation table reports 80.9 on SWE-bench Verified in reasoning mode, near the top open models it compares against. It ships FP8, BF16 and GGUF weights, the base model and intermediate training checkpoints, and a small 37B-A4B sibling. Benchmarks are the team's own.

deck.headline: Banned Nvidia racks surface in Shanghai, tied to Alice Huang's Megaspeed, Bloomberg finds
deck.summary: Bloomberg found a banned Nvidia GB300 rack pledged as loan collateral by a Shanghai firm tied to Megaspeed, the blacklisted Singapore partner founded by Alice Huang. The FT reported Nvidia halted shipments to South-East Asia; Singapore says that is unconfirmed. Jensen Huang faces House questions on 1 December.
deck.whyItMatters: Physical evidence of banned chips in China sharpens the export-control case against Nvidia's partner network, days before Huang's testimony.
deck.update: Bloomberg traces a banned GB300 rack to a Shanghai data centre tied to Megaspeed; FT says Nvidia halted South-East Asia shipments (Singapore calls that unconfirmed)
deck.detailHtml: Loan documents filed with Chinese regulators show a GB300-NVL72 rack, which may not be sold to China, pledged as collateral for a 96m yuan ($14m) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank to Shanghai Shuoyao, Bloomberg reports; it traced the rack through a serial number to Gigabyte. Bloomberg links Shuoyao to Megaspeed, the Singapore firm founded by Alice Huang that became Nvidia's biggest South-East Asian customer and was blacklisted by the US this month. The FT separately reported that Nvidia had halted chip shipments to South-East Asia; Singapore says that is unconfirmed and is in talks with Washington to keep access. Nvidia rose 0.8% to $150.49 on Friday; Jensen Huang faces House committee questions on 1 Dec.

alsoToday.summary: The PolinRider campaign, linked to North Korea, has compromised more than 7,600 GitHub repositories, possibly since February 2025, The Hacker News reports. Its latest trick is a Python loader planted in 375 public repositories belonging to 260 accounts that runs when developers clone and run or import a project.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: With SAP and 1Password both breached through GitHub this week, treat developer accounts and cloned code as an attack surface.

alsoToday.whyItMatters: Plan seats on real usage, not launch-week allowances.

alsoToday.summary: FINMA has approved UBS's 2025 recovery plan, its first approval since the Credit Suisse takeover, and found the bank easier to resolve as the integration advanced; its preferred strategy, a bail-in to rebuild capital, can be carried out, FintechNews reports.

alsoToday.headline: China sets rules for blockchain digital IDs, effective March 2027
alsoToday.summary: Eleven Chinese agencies including the People's Bank of China issued rules for blockchain-based digital identities on the national blockchain network, run by entities the cyberspace regulator authorises; they take effect on 1 March 2027, Cointelegraph reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A state-run identity layer that banks and platforms in China will be expected to plug into for KYC.

alsoToday.headline: Spain moves to let its AML unit freeze crypto accounts without a judge
alsoToday.summary: A decree published on 25 Nov would let Sepblac, Spain's financial intelligence unit, freeze crypto accounts for up to five business days and hold transactions for up to ten without prior judicial approval when it suspects money laundering or terrorist financing, Cointelegraph reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Spain's election on Sunday decides who votes on it.

alsoToday.summary: FIFA told the AP that criminals got into its systems and took 'a limited set of personal and business information', and that it is working with law enforcement. A group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club had posted screenshots of alleged FIFA files a week earlier.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: With the 2030 World Cup planning under way, expect phishing that uses leaked FIFA data.

alsoToday.headline: Thanksgiving storms leave 360,000 US homes without power

alsoToday.headline: Citi's $35bn booking error leads to a management shake-up, WSJ says
alsoToday.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports that Citigroup's $35bn bookkeeping error, trades misbooked at a European trading unit that understated its risk-weighted assets, has led to a shake-up in its upper ranks. We could only read the headline; names and roles are not confirmed here.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Citi is still under consent orders over data and risk controls, so another controls failure tests regulators' patience as it seeks to close them.

alsoToday.headline: UniCredit to put Orcel forward as Commerzbank chair, FT reports
alsoToday.summary: UniCredit intends to propose its chief executive Andrea Orcel as chair of Commerzbank, the FT reports. UniCredit has close to half of Commerzbank's voting rights and said this month it would call a shareholder vote on a new board once it takes control; Reuters reported on 18-19 Nov that UniCredit and Berlin had settled the main sticking points.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Orcel chairing the target would put Europe's biggest cross-border bank merger in years under one man's direct control.
